To understand the efficiency bottlenecks in modern large language model inference, it is necessary to look at how tokens are generated. In standard autoregressive decoding, every new token requires a full forward pass through the entire network to update the internal state and sample the next word. This process is fundamentally serial and heavily constrained by memory bandwidth, as the model must constantly read massive parameter matrices and intermediate activations from high-bandwidth memory. Speculative decoding was introduced to break this sequential dependency by decoupling the generation of candidate tokens from their final verification. The core insight is that a small, fast "draft" model can propose a sequence of likely upcoming tokens in a single step, and these candidates can be checked by the large "target" model in one parallel batch. Instead of waiting for N individual forward passes to produce N tokens, the system performs one pass for the draft and one pass for the target to potentially accept all N tokens at once, effectively trading compute for latency.

The mechanism relies on a probabilistic rejection sampling technique to ensure that the output distribution of the target model is preserved exactly, even though the draft model is much less capable.
